Data not available in repository. 

The specific oxygen concentration used during DAFT-2 (Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test-2) cannot be reported because:
1. There is no source document for DAFT-2 available in the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository.
2. The oxygen concentration parameters (`o2_min`, `o2_max`, `o2_raw`) for DAFT-2 are completely unknown.

Furthermore, the Golden Table entry referencing DAFT-2 is an unverified LLM draft where all test variables (including fuel parameters, ambient pressure, flow velocity, and oxygen limits) are listed as unknown.

### Related Context on Oxygen Concentration in the Repository
* **Microgravity Flammability:** Material flammability depends strongly on oxygen concentration and convective air flow velocity [F-007].
* **Highest O₂ Testing:** The highest oxygen concentrations tested in microgravity within the available repository data were conducted under the ACME Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G), which utilized an oxidizer stream containing up to 85% oxygen [F-018].
* **Lunar Habitat Standards:** Anticipated intermediate atmospheres for lunar surface extravehicular activities (EVAs) target oxygen concentrations of 30% or higher at total pressures of 10.2 psi or lower [F-005] to reduce pre-breathe times [F-004], representing more than a 40% increase in oxygen concentration compared to Earth's atmosphere [F-006].

facts.claim: To reduce pre-breathe times and facilitate lunar surface extravehicular activities (EVAs), the atmosphere in lunar habitats and pressurized rovers is anticipated to have pressure and oxygen concentration intermediate between spacesuits and Earth sea-level atmosphere.
The intermediate atmosphere for lunar operations is anticipated to feature an oxygen concentration of 30% or higher, with a total pressure of 10.2 psi or lower.
According to the challenge text, this represents more than a 40% increase in oxygen concentration compared to Earth's atmosphere, substantially increasing material flammability.
Flammability depends strongly on oxygen concentration; in microgravity, convective air flow speed is also critical.

The highest oxygen concentration combustion tests in microgravity were conducted under ACME's Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G). The combustion chamber was charged with nitrogen and fuel gas (e.g., propane), while an oxidizer stream containing up to 85% oxygen was delivered through a spherical porous burner to create an inverse diffusion flame.

[Saffire-II | S-020: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire) | B. Diagnostics]
This material will be expected to burn at the anticipated oxygen mole fraction of the
cabin atmosphere (near 0.21 O mole fraction). A second redundant igniter is woven into the fabric at the downstream end of the sample in case of a failure of the upstream igniter or if the flame does not propagate the
entire length of the sample. The objective of the tests to be conducted on Saffire-II is to investigate the low-gravity
Maximum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) flammability limits in long-term low gravity.2 The configuration for these
experiments consists of nine samples of varying materials (denoted flammability samples) each having dimensions
of approximately 5 cm wide by 29 cm long installed on the same panel in place of the single sample in Fig. 1. The
Saffire-II sample card is shown in Fig. 2b. These samples emulate the configuration used in NASA-STD-6001 Test
1.3 Each sample is ignited at the bottom using a hot wire. The oxygen concentration in the Cygnus vehicle will be
nearly 21% by volume—the same as in the ISS when the hatch was closed. The materials have been selected to be
near their normal-gravity or hypothesized low-gravity maximum oxygen concentration in 21% O . This has complicated the selection of sample materials because most materials relevant for spacecraft do not have normal-gravity flammability limits near 21% oxygen by volume.4-6 Camera images are the primary diagnostics for these
tests as the intended result is primarily to determine whether the flame propagates or self-extinguishes.

[BASS-II | S-007: NASA/TM-20210011385 BASS-II Summary Report | 5.4 Oxygen Concentration Analysis]
5.4 Oxygen Concentration Analysis
The BASS hardware does not have a provision to measure O concentration throughout the entire experiment. We have O data available at only the start and end of the test. Assuming a linear profile between these two points; we made O concentration graphs for each test (see Figure 5.2 for an example). This helps us estimate the O concentration at any given time during the experiment. Next, the average O
2 2
concentration was calculated for each flow speed. Plots were created summarizing the average O concentration (vol%) versus opposed-flow speed (cm/s) for the one-sided and two-sided tests separately. The data points on these graphs are characterized according to the flame spread rate. Additionally, the
data points at which the flame extinguishes are also added to the summary graphs to see the effects of
varying O concentration through the duration of test. This analysis will serve as a reference point when more BASS operations are conducted in the future. 5.5 Numerical Modeling
We are modeling combustion of flat PMMA samples in microgravity using Fire Dynamics Simulator
(FDS; v5.5.3; National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)) (Ref. 12), which is a
computational fluid dynamics model of fire-driven fluid flow. The entire modeling for BASS–II is done
in Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) mode because of the laminar conditions and small domain. The
model employs the same test sample and approximate BASS flow duct geometry as the experiment.

[BASS-II | S-008: BASS-2 Engineering Requirements | BASS-2 Engineering Requirements]
BASS-2 Engineering Requirements
Acceleration
BASS-2 testing will be scheduled around planned thruster firing or spacecraft dock or undock. The acceleration environment will be measured by the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) during BASS-2 testing which will be installed into the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) Work Volume. Oxygen Concentration
The BASS-2 experiment will include steps in crew procedures to install a Compound Specific Analyzer (CSA-O2) into the MSG to measure the Oxygen concentration. There is also a Major Constituent Analyzer available to measure the Columbus Module concentration. Crew inserts fuel sample and adjusts igniter and fuel base to desired position
Sample Frame Assembly is designed to allow for adjustment of the position of the BASS-2 solid fuel sample. The Igniter has a wire extension that the crew will be able to position as required to ignite the solid fuel sample. 4/14/2010

rules.rule: Do NOT extrapolate microgravity results directly to Lunar or Martian gravity without explicitly stating the lack of direct partial-gravity empirical data and explaining bounding logic ([F-019], [F-021]).

When queried regarding combustion in Lunar or Martian gravity, explicitly clarify that NASA PSI currently contains no partial-gravity test data [F-019]. Mention E-FIELD electric field chemi-ion simulation [F-020] and 0-g/1-g bounding methodology [F-021] if relevant.

Never assess spacecraft fire flammability solely on oxygen percentage. Always evaluate oxygen partial pressure (via calculation), total pressure, diluent inert species (N2, CO2, He), and ventilation forced flow velocity together.
If asked about rocket engine or thruster propellant fires, clearly state that propulsion systems are outside the scope of PSI microgravity science due to momentum-dominated flow regimes [F-022].

For every experimental finding reported, cite the exact test conditions: fuel type, geometry, oxygen concentration, ambient pressure, flow velocity, and hardware facility. If a condition is omitted in the source, label it as 'unspecified'; do NOT guess.
If an empirical value or data point is absent from the indexed chunks and Golden Table, state 'data not available in repository'. Never fabricate numerical values from LLM parametric memory.
When source documents report conflicting findings or values, present both sources with their respective document citations, PI names, and publication years; do not arbitrarily select one.

Clearly distinguish between empirical flight experiment findings (PSI / peer-reviewed reports), challenge guidelines, mathematical derivations, and speculative engineering hypotheses. Never present interpretation as an empirical fact.
